questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall which aging skin changes are expected and which findings make a wound an acute problem.
questions.hintStrategy: Use actual versus potential and acute versus chronic to rank the findings.
questions.stem: An 84-year-old resident of a long-term care facility with type 2 diabetes bumped her arm on a wheelchair armrest during a transfer. During the nurse's skin assessment, which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
options: Flat purple patches on both forearms that appear after minor bumps
Dry, flaky skin on both lower legs with scattered scratch marks
An open 4-cm skin tear on the left forearm that is oozing blood
Eats about 30–40% of meals and has an albumin of 3.0 g/dL
optionRationales: Incorrect. These are senile purpura, an expected aging change from fragile vessels.
Incorrect. Dry skin with scratch marks needs a care plan (mild cleanser, moisturizer, short nails), but it is not urgent.
Correct. An open, bleeding skin tear is an actual, acute break in the barrier. It needs bleeding control and wound care now.
Incorrect. Poor intake and low albumin will slow healing and need a dietitian referral, but this is an ongoing problem, not an immediate one.
questions.rationale: Thin older skin tears easily when bumped, and a skin tear is an unintentional, open wound. Several findings need attention, but the actively bleeding skin tear is an actual, acute threat: it is losing blood and is open to infection. Senile purpura is expected with aging, and dry skin and poor nutrition are chronic problems to plan for after the wound is managed.
questions.takeaway: Actual, acute, bleeding wound first; expected aging changes and chronic problems next.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Diagnostics, Labs & Nursing Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall how each lab on the slides affects healing and how aging changes healing time.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each result with its reference range. Keep only findings that are abnormal or known to slow healing.
questions.stem: An 84-year-old resident with type 2 diabetes has a 4-cm skin tear on the forearm. She eats about 30–40% of meals and has showered daily in hot water with deodorant soap for years. Refer to the Laboratory Results. Which findings are likely to delay healing of the skin tear? Select all that apply.
options: Albumin 3.0 g/dL
Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL
Fasting glucose 168 mg/dL
Age of 84 years
WBC 7,800/mm³
Platelets 210,000/mm³
optionRationales: Correct. Albumin below 3.5 g/dL reflects poor nutrition, which delays healing and raises infection risk.
Correct. Low hemoglobin means less oxygen is delivered to healing tissue.
Correct. High blood glucose slows healing and feeds bacteria.
Correct. Older adults have thinner skin and an increased healing time.
Incorrect. The WBC is normal, so infection defense is adequate.
Incorrect. The platelet count is normal.
questions.rationale: Healing needs protein and calories, oxygen, a working immune system, and normal glucose. This resident has low albumin (poor nutrition, also shown by her low intake), low hemoglobin (less oxygen delivery), high glucose, and advanced age, which by itself increases healing time. The normal WBC and platelet values are distractors.
questions.takeaway: Low albumin, low Hgb, high glucose, and older age all slow healing; normal values are distractors.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Recall which oil-producing structures decrease with age and how often the slides say older adults should bathe.
questions.hintStrategy: Find the root cause of the dry skin in the stem, then choose the change that removes it.
questions.stem: An 84-year-old resident has thin, dry, itchy skin with scratch marks on both lower legs. She says she has showered every day in hot water with deodorant soap “my whole life.” Which change to her hygiene routine is the priority for the nurse to recommend?
options: Continue daily showers but switch to an antibacterial soap to prevent infection
Shower every other day in lukewarm water with a mild cleanser, then moisturize
Shower twice daily in cool water to relieve the itching on her legs
Continue daily hot showers and apply an alcohol-based lotion to her legs
optionRationales: Incorrect. Daily washing with harsh soap strips oil from skin that already has fewer oil glands.
Correct. Older adults have fewer sebaceous glands, so hot water and harsh soap dry the skin. The slides recommend bathing every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser, then moisturizing.
Incorrect. More frequent bathing increases dryness, which worsens the itching.
Incorrect. Hot water dries the skin, and alcohol-based products worsen dryness.
questions.rationale: Aging reduces sebaceous (oil) glands, so older skin is dry and itchy, and scratching can break the barrier. Hot water, deodorant soap, and daily bathing all strip the remaining oils. The slides recommend bathing older adults every other day with lukewarm water and a mild or liquid cleanser, patting dry, and moisturizing right after the bath.
questions.takeaway: Older adults: bathe every other day, lukewarm water, mild cleanser, moisturize.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Recall safe handling of fragile older skin, infection prevention during wound care, and the nutrients for healing.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option true or false. Reject any action that creates friction or pulls on the skin.
questions.stem: An 84-year-old resident who uses a wheelchair has thin skin, senile purpura, a dressed skin tear on the forearm, and an albumin of 3.0 g/dL. She usually wears short-sleeved shirts. The nurse is planning care to protect her skin and promote healing. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Pad the wheelchair armrests and use a draw sheet with two staff to reposition her
Encourage her to wear long-sleeved clothing
Secure the forearm dressing with standard adhesive tape
Request a dietitian consult for more calories, protein, and vitamins A and C
Perform hand hygiene before and after dressing changes and discard soiled dressings safely
Pull her up in bed by the arms to avoid pressure on the sacrum
optionRationales: Correct. Padding hard surfaces and lifting with a draw sheet prevent friction, bruises, and new tears.
Correct. Long sleeves protect fragile forearm skin from bumps.
Incorrect. Adhesive tape can tear fragile skin when removed. Tape-free options are preferred.
Correct. Albumin below 3.5 g/dL reflects poor nutrition. Protein, calories, and vitamins A and C support healing.
Correct. Hand hygiene and safe disposal of dressings prevent wound infection.
Incorrect. Pulling by the arms causes friction and can tear skin and bruise the arms.
questions.rationale: The plan connects aging changes, wound care, and nutrition. Thin skin and fragile vessels call for padding, long sleeves, lifting instead of pulling, and no tape. The open skin tear needs infection prevention: hand hygiene before and after care and safe disposal of soiled dressings. The low albumin calls for more protein, calories, and vitamins A and C with a dietitian consult.
questions.takeaway: Protect fragile skin, prevent wound infection, and feed the wound.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Wound Types & Classification
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall the order of care for a fresh, bleeding wound and how fragile older skin changes technique.
questions.hintStrategy: All options may be done at some point. Choose the one that addresses the most immediate problem.
questions.stem: An 84-year-old resident with thin, fragile skin has a new 4-cm skin tear on the forearm that is oozing bright red blood. After performing hand hygiene and putting on gloves, which action should the nurse take first?
options: Clean the skin tear with normal saline
Apply gentle pressure with gauze and elevate the arm
Cover the skin tear with a nonadherent dressing and a wrap
Complete an incident report about the transfer
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cleaning comes after bleeding is controlled.
Correct. Controlling bleeding comes first. Gentle pressure protects fragile skin, and elevation slows blood flow to the wound.
Incorrect. Covering comes after bleeding is controlled and the wound is cleaned.
Incorrect. Documentation is needed, but it comes after the client's immediate needs are met.
questions.rationale: The first-aid order for an untreated wound applies to a skin tear: control bleeding with pressure and elevation, then clean with saline, then cover. Because aging skin is thin and fragile, the nurse uses gentle pressure and chooses a nonadherent, tape-free dressing afterward.
questions.takeaway: Skin tear: gentle pressure and elevation first, then clean and cover without tape.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Recall safe repositioning for fragile skin and the UAP's role on the skin care team.
questions.hintStrategy: Three options show goals met. Find the finding that shows new harm.
questions.stem: Two weeks after a skin-protection plan was started for an 84-year-old resident with fragile skin, the nurse reviews the findings. Which finding indicates the need for the nurse's immediate follow-up?
options: Lower legs soft and moisturized, with no new scratch marks
Skin tear on the forearm closed, with no drainage or redness
Now showers every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser
New upper-arm bruise after a UAP pulled her up by the arms
optionRationales: Incorrect. This shows the moisturizing goal is met.
Incorrect. This shows the wound has healed without infection.
Incorrect. This shows the hygiene goal is met.
Correct. Pulling by the arms causes friction and injures fragile skin. The nurse must assess the bruise and correct the UAP's technique (lift with a draw sheet) now.
questions.rationale: Evaluation checks each goal separately. Three findings show goals met. The new bruise shows the plan is not being followed: pulling fragile skin causes bruising and tears. UAPs do the turning and repositioning, so the RN must follow up by assessing the client and reinforcing safe technique (lift, don't drag).
questions.takeaway: Evaluate each goal separately; a new injury from unsafe handling needs follow-up now.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Identify the type of rash from its shape, timing, and history. Recall how topical steroids are safely applied.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option as true or false. Eliminate treatments meant for infections.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Clinic, 1015: 38-year-old client reports an intensely itchy rash that started 2 days after dyeing her hair at home with a new permanent hair dye. She used a different dye of the same color 3 months ago and had mild itching afterward. Assessment: red, swollen skin with small vesicles along the hairline, forehead, tops of the ears, and back of the neck, ending sharply where the dye touched the skin. No crusting or drainage. No lesions elsewhere. Denies shortness of breath or throat tightness. No one at home has a rash.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Which actions should the nurse take for this client? Select all that apply.
options: Teach the client to avoid the hair dye and document the allergy
Place the client on contact precautions
Apply cool compresses and a thin layer of the prescribed topical corticosteroid
Apply an antifungal cream to the rash twice daily
Monitor the intensity of itching and the extent of redness and vesicles
Cover the rash with an occlusive dressing overnight
optionRationales: Correct. The rash is allergic contact dermatitis. Avoiding the allergen prevents recurrence, and documenting it protects the client.
Incorrect. Allergic contact dermatitis is not infectious. Nothing suggests impetigo or another contagious rash.
Correct. Cool compresses and a thin layer of topical corticosteroid reduce inflammation and itching.
Incorrect. The pattern is not fungal (no scaly ring), so an antifungal will not help.
Correct. Itching and rash extent show whether the reaction is improving.
Incorrect. Occlusion increases steroid absorption and is not used unless prescribed.
questions.rationale: A vesicular rash that ends sharply where the dye touched the skin, appearing days after exposure in a client already sensitized by earlier dye use, is allergic contact dermatitis. It is not infectious, so precautions and antifungals do not apply. Care is to avoid and document the allergen, reduce inflammation with cool compresses and a thin, uncovered layer of topical corticosteroid, and monitor the response.
questions.takeaway: Allergic contact dermatitis is not contagious: avoid the allergen, apply a thin layer of steroid, and monitor.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall the expected skin changes of aging, the ABCDE rule, and the bruise patterns that suggest abuse.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding as expected with aging or unexpected. Select only the unexpected ones.

tabs.title: History
tabs.html: 84-year-old client with hypertension and osteoarthritis. Lives with an adult son who is the primary caregiver. Medications: amlodipine, acetaminophen PRN. Home health nurse's first visit.

questions.stem: The home health nurse is performing a skin assessment. Refer to the History. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Thin, translucent skin with visible veins on the backs of both hands
Flat, dark purple patches on the forearms that appear with the smallest bump
Several oval bruises in different stages of healing on both inner upper arms
Multiple waxy, brown, “stuck-on” raised lesions on the back
A 9-mm dark mole on the left calf with a notched border that seems bigger
A pearly sore on the right ear rim that has bled on and off for 2 months
optionRationales: Incorrect. Thin, translucent skin is an expected aging change from fewer melanocytes and a thinner dermis.
Incorrect. These are senile purpura, expected with fragile aging vessels.
Correct. Bruises in different stages in a protected area (inner arms) may indicate abuse and must be documented objectively and reported.
Incorrect. Waxy, stuck-on lesions that are not changing are typically benign growths common in older adults.
Correct. A mole with an irregular border, a diameter over 6 mm, and evolving size meets ABCDE criteria for possible melanoma.
Correct. A pearly, bleeding sore that won't heal on a sun-exposed area suggests basal cell carcinoma.
questions.rationale: Knowing normal aging lets the nurse pick out what is not normal. Thin skin, senile purpura, and stable stuck-on lesions are expected. Bruises in different stages in protected areas suggest possible abuse. A mole meeting ABCDE criteria and a pearly sore that bleeds and won't heal suggest skin cancer and need referral.
questions.takeaway: Expected aging vs. red flags: patterned bruises, ABCDE moles, and non-healing sores need follow-up.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Wound Types & Classification
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall the signs of shock after a bleeding wound.
questions.hintStrategy: Use ABCs: which finding shows a threat to circulation?
questions.stem: A 45-year-old client is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after falling through a glass door. A pressure dressing has been applied to a deep laceration on the right forearm. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
options: Restlessness with a weak pulse of 128/min and BP of 86/54 mm Hg
Pain rated 5/10 at the forearm laceration
Small abrasions on both knees with a small amount of serous oozing
Closed, swollen bruise on the right hip
optionRationales: Correct. Restlessness, a rapid weak pulse, and low BP are signs of shock from blood loss.
Incorrect. Moderate pain is expected and should be treated, but it is not life-threatening.
Incorrect. Minor abrasions with serous oozing are not urgent.
Incorrect. A contusion needs ice and monitoring but is not the priority.
questions.rationale: After a wound with heavy bleeding, the nurse watches for shock: rapid, weak pulse; cool, clammy skin; low BP; and restlessness or confusion. These findings require immediate action (maintain pressure and elevation, lay flat, call for help, and anticipate IV fluids).
questions.takeaway: ↑ HR, ↓ BP, and restlessness after a wound = shock until proven otherwise.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Structure & Function
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall how the skin makes vitamin D and how melanin and aging affect that process.
questions.hintStrategy: Count the risk factors each client has. Choose the client with the most.
questions.stem: The clinic nurse is reviewing four clients' histories during intake. Which client has the greatest risk for vitamin D deficiency related to reduced skin synthesis?
options: A 24-year-old lifeguard with light skin who uses SPF 30 sunscreen
A 45-year-old landscaper with medium skin who works outside year-round
A 16-year-old soccer player with dark skin who practices outdoors daily
An 86-year-old homebound client with dark skin
optionRationales: Incorrect. This client gets a lot of sun exposure, and young skin makes vitamin D efficiently.
Incorrect. Year-round outdoor work provides ample UV exposure.
Incorrect. Daily outdoor activity offsets the effect of more melanin.
Correct. Older age, darker skin (more melanin blocks UV), and little sun exposure each reduce vitamin D production, so this client has three risks at once.
questions.rationale: The skin makes vitamin D when UV light strikes it. Melanin absorbs UV, so darker skin makes less vitamin D for the same sun exposure. Aging skin also makes less, and homebound clients get little sun. The client who combines all three risks is at highest risk.
questions.takeaway: Older age + darker skin + little sun = highest risk for low vitamin D.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Structure & Function
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall which skin function is lost with neuropathy and what the client must use instead.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a negatively worded item: find the statement that relies on the lost function.
questions.stem: The nurse has taught a client with diabetic peripheral neuropathy how to protect the skin of the feet. Monofilament testing shows absent sensation on both soles. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I will test my bath water by dipping my foot in before I get in.”
“I will look at the bottoms of my feet with a mirror every night.”
“I will wear shoes or slippers even when I'm inside the house.”
“I will shake out my shoes and feel inside them before I put them on.”
optionRationales: Correct. This needs more teaching. Without sensation, the client cannot feel hot water and could be burned. Use a thermometer or the elbow.
Incorrect. Daily visual inspection replaces the lost warning of pain.
Incorrect. Wearing footwear protects feet the client cannot feel.
Incorrect. Checking shoes by hand finds objects the feet cannot feel.
questions.rationale: The dermis contains nerve endings that sense pain, pressure, and temperature. Neuropathy removes this warning, so the client must replace feeling with looking and with safer tools. Any plan that relies on the feet to feel temperature or injury is unsafe.
questions.takeaway: With neuropathy, replace feeling with looking; never test water with the feet.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Structure & Function
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall the five skin functions and what the client experiences when each one fails.
questions.hintStrategy: Match each option to the function that failed, then pick the temperature one.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing several clients with problems related to skin function. Which client's finding reflects impaired temperature regulation by the skin?
options: A client with a spinal cord injury does not notice a hot drink spilled on the lap
An 88-year-old with little subcutaneous fat shivers in a room staff find comfortable
A client with extensive open abrasions from a motorcycle crash develops a wound infection
A client with diabetic neuropathy does not notice a blister from new shoes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Not noticing a spill reflects loss of sensation.
Correct. Loss of subcutaneous fat with aging reduces insulation, and aging skin regulates temperature less well, so the client feels cold.
Incorrect. Infection reflects loss of the protective barrier.
Incorrect. An unnoticed blister reflects loss of sensation.
questions.rationale: Each skin function fails in a recognizable way. The protection function fails as infection or fluid loss; the sensation function fails as unnoticed injury; temperature regulation fails as overheating or getting cold easily. In older adults, reduced subcutaneous fat and less responsive vessels make it hard to stay warm.
questions.takeaway: Older adult + little subcutaneous fat + always cold = impaired temperature regulation.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Structure & Function
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Recall what gives the dermis its strength and which medication classes thin the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Link the medication in the stem to the skin layer it affects.
questions.stem: A 67-year-old client with COPD has taken prednisone 20 mg PO daily for 2 years. The nurse notes thin, shiny skin on the forearms with several purple bruises and a healing skin tear. Which explanation for these findings is most accurate?
options: Chronic hypoxemia from COPD has reduced melanin production in the epidermis
Hypothyroidism has reduced sebum secretion from the oil glands of the skin
Long-term steroid use has thinned the dermis and weakened its collagen
Excess vitamin C intake has made the blood vessels of the skin fragile
optionRationales: Incorrect. Melanin affects color and UV protection, not skin strength or bruising.
Incorrect. Nothing suggests hypothyroidism, and reduced sebum causes dry skin, not bruising.
Correct. Steroids are among the medications that thin the skin. They weaken collagen in the dermis, so small vessels lose support and skin tears and bruises easily.
Incorrect. Vitamin C is needed to make collagen. It does not cause fragile vessels.
questions.rationale: The dermis contains collagen and blood vessels. Long-term steroids, one of the medication classes that thin the skin, weaken collagen so vessels lose support, producing thin, shiny skin, easy bruising, and skin tears. The nurse handles the skin gently, lifts instead of dragging, pads surfaces, and avoids tape.
questions.takeaway: Long-term steroids thin the dermis: expect bruising and skin tears.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall where to look for jaundice in darker skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the site with the least melanin that also shows bilirubin staining.
questions.stem: A client with deeply pigmented skin is admitted with suspected hepatitis. Total bilirubin is 4.8 mg/dL. The nurse notes a slight yellowish tint at the outer edges of the sclera. Which assessment should the nurse perform next to confirm jaundice?
options: Press on the nail beds and time the capillary refill
Inspect the lower eyelid conjunctiva for pallor
Compare the skin color on the chest with the forearms
Inspect the hard palate and the palms of the hands
optionRationales: Incorrect. Capillary refill assesses peripheral circulation, not jaundice.
Incorrect. The conjunctiva is checked for pallor, not jaundice.
Incorrect. Pigmented skin can hide a yellow tint.
Correct. In dark skin, jaundice is confirmed in low-pigment areas such as the hard palate, palms, and soles, not the sclera alone.
questions.rationale: The outer sclera of darkly pigmented clients can look yellowish normally, so the nurse confirms jaundice in other low-pigment areas: the hard palate, palms, and soles.
questions.takeaway: Jaundice in dark skin: sclera plus hard palate, palms, and soles.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall what a wheal indicates and which accompanying symptom turns a skin finding into an airway problem.
questions.hintStrategy: Use ABCs. Look for a skin finding linked to a threat to the airway.
questions.stem: The nurse receives hand-off report on four clients with skin findings. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with new raised wheals on the trunk who reports a hoarse voice
A client with psoriasis who has silvery, scaly plaques on both elbows
An older adult with several waxy, stuck-on brown papules on the upper back
An adolescent with scattered pustules on the forehead and chin
optionRationales: Correct. Wheals (hives) with a hoarse voice suggest an allergic reaction affecting the airway, an emergency.
Incorrect. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory disorder and is not an emergency.
Incorrect. Stable, stuck-on lesions in an older adult are usually benign.
Incorrect. Acne pustules are a common adolescent inflammatory disorder, not urgent.
questions.rationale: Most inflammatory skin disorders, such as psoriasis and acne, are chronic or uncomfortable but not dangerous. Wheals, a primary lesion of allergic reactions, become an emergency when paired with hoarseness, wheezing, or throat tightness, because the airway is involved. Airway comes first.
questions.takeaway: Hives + hoarseness = airway emergency; see that client first.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall the history questions and lesion features that make up a focused skin assessment.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each action is within the nurse's scope and safe for the skin.
questions.stem: A client comes to the clinic with a rash on the torso that began 4 days ago. Which data should the nurse collect during the focused skin assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Size of representative lesions measured in millimeters or centimeters
Distribution and arrangement of the lesions (for example, linear, clustered, or scattered)
Any new medications, soaps, foods, or exposures before the rash appeared
The content of a pustule obtained by squeezing it onto gauze
Associated symptoms such as itching, pain, or fever
The likely diagnosis based on the appearance of the rash
optionRationales: Correct. Measurable size allows accurate documentation and comparison.
Correct. The pattern and location help identify the cause.
Correct. New exposures point to allergic or irritant causes.
Incorrect. The nurse does not squeeze or pop lesions.
Correct. Symptoms add important clues and can signal a systemic problem.
Incorrect. The nurse describes and reports; the provider diagnoses.
questions.rationale: A focused skin assessment includes a history (onset, symptoms, new exposures, home remedies) and a description of the lesions (type, size, color, shape, distribution, drainage). The nurse describes and reports findings without squeezing lesions or diagnosing.
questions.takeaway: Describe, don't diagnose; measure, map, and ask about exposures.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall how a Wood lamp works and what can interfere with it.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that describe a different test.
questions.stem: A client with several sharply defined, milky-white patches on the hands and around the mouth is scheduled for a Wood lamp examination to evaluate for vitiligo. Which instruction should the nurse give before the examination?
options: “Do not eat or drink anything for 8 hours before the examination.”
“Skip lotion, makeup, and creams on your hands and face that day.”
“A small skin sample will be removed after a local anesthetic injection.”
“The lamp will be pressed against your skin in a brightly lit room.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A Wood lamp exam is noninvasive and needs no fasting.
Correct. Lotions, makeup, and creams can glow under UV light and confuse the result.
Incorrect. That describes a biopsy, not a Wood lamp exam.
Incorrect. The exam uses a handheld UV light near the skin in a darkened room.
questions.rationale: Loss of pigment (vitiligo) shows up clearly under the ultraviolet light of a Wood lamp, which is held near the skin in a darkened room. It is painless. Products on the skin can fluoresce and create false results, so the area should be clean and product-free.
questions.takeaway: Wood lamp: dark room, painless, no lotions or makeup on the area.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Recall how impetigo spreads and how long the child remains contagious after treatment starts.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the transmission route to the type of precaution.
questions.stem: A 6-year-old admitted for asthma is found to have honey-crusted lesions on the chin that are diagnosed as impetigo. A topical antibiotic is started today. Which infection control measure should the nurse implement?
options: Droplet precautions until all of the crusted lesions have healed
Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room for 48 hours
Contact precautions until 24 hours of effective therapy
Standard precautions only, with the lesions left open to air
optionRationales: Incorrect. Impetigo is not spread by droplets.
Incorrect. Airborne precautions are for organisms such as varicella.
Correct. Impetigo spreads by direct contact, so contact precautions are used until 24 hours of effective treatment.
Incorrect. Standard precautions alone are not enough for a contagious contact-spread infection.
questions.rationale: Impetigo is a contagious bacterial infection spread by direct contact. Gown and gloves (contact precautions) are used until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy.
questions.takeaway: Impetigo: contact precautions until 24 hours of treatment.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Recall how scabies spreads and how treatment is applied.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option as true or false. Watch for partial treatments.
questions.stem: In a long-term care facility, a resident is diagnosed with scabies, and two staff members who provided care report new itching. The charge nurse is coordinating the facility's response. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Place the resident on contact precautions with gown and gloves for direct care
Arrange for the resident and exposed staff to be treated at the same time
Wash the resident's recently used bedding and clothing in hot water and dry on high heat
Remove precautions as soon as the resident reports that the itching has stopped
Seal items that cannot be washed in a plastic bag for several days
Apply the scabicide cream only to the areas where burrows are visible
optionRationales: Correct. Scabies spreads by skin-to-skin contact.
Correct. Treating all contacts together prevents mites passing back and forth.
Correct. Hot washing and high-heat drying kill mites on linens.
Incorrect. Itching can last 2–4 weeks after successful treatment, so it is not a guide to ending precautions.
Correct. Mites die when sealed away from a host for several days.
Incorrect. The scabicide is applied from the neck to the toes, not only to visible burrows.
questions.rationale: Scabies mites spread through prolonged skin contact and sometimes linens. The response is contact precautions, simultaneous treatment of the resident and all symptomatic contacts, whole-body application of the scabicide, and hot laundering or bagging of items. Itching may persist for weeks after cure.
questions.takeaway: Scabies: treat everyone at once, neck to toes, hot wash or bag, and expect lingering itch.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall how normal wound drainage differs from infected drainage and which finding suggests infection is spreading.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for a combination of local and systemic signs. Chronic stable conditions are distractors.
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical-surgical unit is reviewing four clients with skin and wound findings. Which client's findings require the nurse's immediate attention?
options: A client with athlete's foot who reports itching and scaling between the toes
A client with psoriasis who has silvery, scaly, itchy plaques on both elbows and both knees
A client with a knee abrasion that has a small amount of clear, serous oozing
A client whose incision has new purulent drainage and a fever of 38.9 °C (102 °F)
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tinea pedis in a healthy client is uncomfortable but not urgent.
Incorrect. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory disorder, not an emergency.
Incorrect. Clear, serous drainage can be normal in an early wound.
Correct. New pus plus fever suggests a wound infection that may be spreading beyond the skin and needs prompt reporting.
questions.rationale: When comparing skin problems, separate chronic or localized conditions (psoriasis, tinea, a clean abrasion) from signs of a spreading infection. Purulent drainage marks an infected wound, and fever suggests the infection is becoming systemic, so this client needs immediate attention.
questions.takeaway: Pus + fever at a wound = possible spreading infection; act first.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall the conditions fungi need to grow and how tinea spreads.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option: does it reduce moisture, prevent spread, or complete treatment?
questions.stem: A 35-year-old client who runs daily is diagnosed with tinea pedis and prescribed a topical antifungal cream. Which instructions should the nurse include in the teaching plan? Select all that apply.
options: Dry thoroughly between the toes after bathing
Wear cotton or moisture-wicking socks and change them when damp
Stop the cream as soon as the itching goes away
Wear sandals or shower shoes in locker rooms and public showers
Rotate athletic shoes so each pair can dry out between uses
Share towels only with members of the same household
optionRationales: Correct. Fungi thrive in warm, moist areas.
Correct. Dry socks reduce moisture.
Incorrect. The full course must be finished, or the fungus can return.
Correct. Shower shoes prevent spread and reinfection.
Correct. Letting shoes dry removes the moist environment fungi need.
Incorrect. Towels should not be shared at all.
questions.rationale: Tinea pedis thrives in warm, moist, dark places. Teaching keeps the feet dry, protects them in shared spaces, avoids sharing items, and completes the full course of antifungal even after symptoms improve.
questions.takeaway: Tinea: keep it dry, don't share, and finish the antifungal.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Recall the dressing-change sequence and when hand hygiene is performed.
questions.hintStrategy: Picture the nurse's hands right now and what they carry. Choose the step that protects the clean wound.
questions.stem: A client has a draining infected wound on the thigh and is on contact precautions. Wearing a gown and clean gloves, the nurse removes the soiled dressing and discards it with the gloves in a leak-proof bag. Which action should the nurse take first at this point?
options: Perform hand hygiene and put on a new pair of gloves
Apply the new dressing and label it with the date, time, and initials
Cleanse the wound with normal saline, moving from the center outward
Remove the gown so it does not touch the clean dressing
optionRationales: Correct. After removing a soiled dressing and gloves, the nurse performs hand hygiene and puts on new gloves so the wound's organisms are not carried back to it.
Incorrect. The wound must be cleansed before a new dressing is applied.
Incorrect. Cleansing comes after hand hygiene and clean gloves.
Incorrect. The gown stays on for the rest of the care under contact precautions.
questions.rationale: Infection prevention during wound care connects contact precautions with the general steps of a dressing change: remove the soiled dressing and discard it safely, remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, put on new gloves, cleanse from least to most contaminated, apply the new dressing, then remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and document.
questions.takeaway: Soiled dressing off → hand hygiene and new gloves → cleanse → new dressing.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall which clients are at greatest risk from fungal infections and what a low WBC means for defense and healing.
questions.hintStrategy: All clients have the same infection. Compare their immune status.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing four clients who each have tinea (a fungal skin infection). Which client should the nurse follow up with first because of the greatest risk for a serious complication?
options: A 20-year-old college athlete with athlete's foot and a WBC of 7,600/mm³
A 35-year-old with ringworm on the forearm after adopting a kitten
A 58-year-old on chemotherapy for leukemia with a WBC of 1,900/mm³
A 10-year-old with a scaly patch on the scalp and mild hair loss
optionRationales: Incorrect. A healthy client with a normal WBC can keep a fungal infection on the surface.
Incorrect. Ringworm in a healthy adult is usually mild.
Correct. Chemotherapy and a low WBC make the client immunocompromised. Fungi are most dangerous in immunocompromised clients and can spread deep or into the blood.
Incorrect. Tinea capitis in a healthy child needs treatment but is not the highest risk.
questions.rationale: Fungi are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients because a weak immune system cannot keep the infection on the surface. A low WBC also means poor infection defense and delayed healing, and it can hide the usual signs of infection. This client needs the closest follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Fungal infection + chemotherapy or low WBC = highest risk; report it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall how each childhood skin infection spreads and the safety rules for treatment.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each parent statement as correct or incorrect.
questions.stem: The pediatric clinic nurse has taught several parents about their children's skin infections. Which parent statements indicate understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: “My child with chickenpox can go back to child care once every blister has crusted over.”
“My son shouldn't pick at or bite the warts on his fingers, because that can spread them.”
“I'll give my daughter aspirin to bring down the fever from her chickenpox.”
“I'll keep my child's fingernails short so scratching doesn't spread the impetigo.”
“After the first lice treatment, I won't need to check my child's hair again.”
optionRationales: Correct. The child is no longer contagious once all lesions are crusted.
Correct. Warts (HPV) spread by touch, including picking and biting.
Incorrect. Aspirin during a viral illness is linked to Reye syndrome. Acetaminophen is used.
Correct. Short nails reduce the spread of impetigo by scratching.
Incorrect. The hair should be rechecked in about a week, since a second treatment is often needed.
questions.rationale: Correct parent teaching for childhood skin infections: return to school when chickenpox lesions are crusted, no aspirin for viral illness, avoid picking warts, keep nails short with impetigo, and recheck hair after lice treatment.
questions.takeaway: Chickenpox crusted = back to school; no aspirin; recheck lice.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall what causes the poison ivy rash and how it spreads.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a negatively worded item: find the INCORRECT statement.
questions.stem: A client has linear streaks of itchy vesicles on both forearms 2 days after clearing brush and poison ivy from a yard. After teaching, which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I should wash the gloves and clothes I wore in the yard.”
“Cool compresses and calamine can help calm the itching.”
“If I scratch open these blisters, the fluid will spread the rash.”
“Next time I'll wash my skin with soap and water as soon as I finish yard work.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is correct. Oil on clothing and gloves can cause new rashes.
Incorrect. This is correct. Cool compresses and soothing lotions ease symptoms.
Correct. This needs more teaching. Blister fluid does not spread poison ivy. The plant oil does.
Incorrect. This is correct. Washing promptly removes the oil.
questions.rationale: Poison ivy causes allergic contact dermatitis from the plant's oil. New lesions come from oil still on skin, clothing, tools, or pets, not from blister fluid. Scratching should still be avoided because it can cause infection.
questions.takeaway: Poison ivy spreads by the oil, not the blister fluid.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall the unchangeable and changeable risk factors for skin disorders.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each client into risk or protective factor.
questions.stem: The nurse at a community health fair is screening clients for risk of skin disorders. Which clients have an increased risk? Select all that apply.
options: A 79-year-old whose skin has become thin and heals slowly
A 30-year-old whose parent and sibling have psoriasis
A 55-year-old who has taken oral steroids for 2 years
A 40-year-old with poor nutrition and recent weight loss
A 25-year-old who eats a balanced diet and moisturizes daily
A 35-year-old who uses a mild cleanser and wears sunscreen daily
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults have thinner skin and slower healing.
Correct. Genetics and family history raise risk, and psoriasis runs in families.
Correct. Long-term steroids thin the skin.
Correct. Poor nutrition causes skin changes and delayed healing.
Incorrect. Good nutrition and moisturizing protect the skin.
Incorrect. Gentle cleansing and sun protection are preventive habits.
questions.rationale: Risk factors for skin disorders span the module: aging (thin skin, slow healing), genetics and family history (psoriasis and eczema run in families), medications (steroids thin skin), and poor nutrition. Protective habits such as moisturizing, mild cleansers, and sunscreen lower risk.
questions.takeaway: Age, genetics, medications, and nutrition all raise skin risk.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Recall the adverse effects of long-term topical corticosteroids and why the face is especially vulnerable.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each finding: does it result from thinning skin?
questions.stem: A client has applied over-the-counter hydrocortisone and then a friend's high-potency steroid cream to the face twice daily for 4 months to treat “redness.” Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible adverse effects of prolonged topical corticosteroid use? Select all that apply.
options: Thin, shiny skin on the treated areas
Small, visible blood vessels under the skin
Thickened, leathery plaques with exaggerated skin lines
Yellow, greasy scales on the eyebrows
Easy bruising in the treated areas
Hard, raised scar tissue extending past the original lesions
optionRationales: Correct. Long-term topical steroids thin the skin.
Correct. Thinned skin makes small blood vessels visible.
Incorrect. Thickened, leathery skin comes from chronic rubbing or sun damage, not steroid use.
Incorrect. Greasy scales are not a steroid effect.
Correct. Thin skin with weakened support bruises easily.
Incorrect. A scar spreading past the wound is a keloid.
questions.rationale: Topical corticosteroids calm inflammation but, when overused, thin the skin, especially on the face where the skin is thin and absorbs more. Adverse effects include thin, shiny skin, visible vessels, easy bruising, stretch marks, and lighter patches. Teach clients to use only prescribed steroids, for the time ordered, and never someone else's medicine.
questions.takeaway: Overused topical steroids thin the skin: shiny skin, visible vessels, and bruising.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Recall how benzoyl peroxide is applied and its expected effects.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the statement that is fully correct. Watch for 'more is better' reasoning.
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 17-year-old about starting benzoyl peroxide 5% gel for mild inflammatory acne. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?
options: “I'll scrub my face hard twice a day so the gel can soak in better.”
“The gel can bleach fabric, so I'll use white towels and pillowcases.”
“I'll apply a thick layer of gel to a pimple that shows up before a big event.”
“If my skin gets dry and flaky, the medicine isn't working for me.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Scrubbing worsens irritation and inflammation.
Correct. Benzoyl peroxide bleaches fabric and hair, so white linens are recommended.
Incorrect. A thin layer is applied to the whole affected area, not thick spot treatment.
Incorrect. Mild dryness and peeling are expected at first and do not mean the drug has failed.
questions.rationale: Acne forms when sebum and dead skin plug follicles and bacteria cause inflammation. Benzoyl peroxide, the first-line OTC treatment, kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Teaching: wash gently, apply a thin layer to the whole area, expect some dryness, use white linens because it bleaches, and allow several weeks for improvement.
questions.takeaway: Benzoyl peroxide: thin layer, expect dryness, and it bleaches fabric.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall the key pattern of each childhood rash and the lesion type chickenpox produces.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the sequence of symptoms to the condition.
questions.stem: A 7-year-old is brought to the school nurse with bright red cheeks that look slapped and a lacy, pink rash on the arms. The child had a mild cold last week and is now afebrile and playful. There are no blisters. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options: Fifth disease
Chickenpox
Roseola
Pityriasis rosea
optionRationales: Correct. A mild cold followed by slapped cheeks and a lacy rash on the limbs is the classic pattern of fifth disease.
Incorrect. Chickenpox causes itchy vesicles in different stages, and there are no blisters here.
Incorrect. Roseola causes several days of high fever followed by a rash on the trunk as the fever breaks, mostly in infants and toddlers.
Incorrect. Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch followed by oval patches on the trunk.
questions.rationale: Childhood rashes are identified by pattern. Fifth disease is a mild viral illness: cold symptoms, then a bright red slapped-cheek rash, then a lacy rash on the arms and legs, with the child feeling well. Chickenpox (vesicles in crops), roseola (fever then rash), and pityriasis rosea (herald patch) have different patterns.
questions.takeaway: Slapped cheeks + lacy rash = fifth disease.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Recall what type of contact dermatitis urine and stool cause and which age group reacts most strongly.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that removes the cause.
questions.stem: A 7-month-old has had frequent loose stools for 2 days. The nurse notes red, shiny, irritated skin on the buttocks and genitals where the diaper touches, with the deep skin folds spared. Which instruction should the nurse give the parent?
options: Scrub the area with antibacterial soap at each diaper change
Cover the diaper with plastic pants to keep the moisture in
Change diapers often and keep the skin clean and dry
Leave soiled diapers on longer so the skin can rest between changes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Scrubbing and harsh soap further damage irritated skin.
Incorrect. Plastic pants trap moisture and worsen irritation.
Correct. This is irritant dermatitis from urine and stool. Frequent changes and keeping the skin clean and dry remove the irritant.
Incorrect. Longer contact with stool and urine worsens the damage.
questions.rationale: Diaper dermatitis is an irritant contact dermatitis: urine and stool directly damage the skin, especially with diarrhea, and infants have the strongest irritant response. Redness where the diaper touches, with folds spared, fits this pattern. Care removes the irritant: frequent changes, gentle cleaning, air drying, and a barrier cream if ordered.
questions.takeaway: Diaper rash = irritant dermatitis: change often, keep clean and dry.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.hintContent: Recall the skin-tone considerations after acne and the risks of bleaching creams.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for a response that is therapeutic and safe.
questions.stem: A 16-year-old with dark brown skin has healing acne with dark spots where the pimples were. The teen says, “I hate how I look. I bought a strong skin-bleaching cream online, and I use it twice a day.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Those dark spots are permanent, so the bleaching cream is the only thing that may help them fade.”
“Apply the cream only at night and in a thinner layer so it is less likely to irritate your skin.”
“Try covering the spots with makeup, since acne is just a normal part of being a teenager.”
“That sounds hard. Those creams can harm skin, so let's ask your provider about safer options.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Dark marks after acne are common in darker skin and often fade. Bleaching creams can harm the skin.
Incorrect. This endorses an unsafe product.
Incorrect. This dismisses the teen's feelings and does not address the harmful product.
Correct. This acknowledges the teen's feelings, explains the risk, and redirects to safe treatment.
questions.rationale: Darker skin is more prone to inflammation and often keeps dark marks after acne heals. Bleaching creams can irritate the skin or interact with medications, and darker skin may need a combination treatment plan chosen by a provider. For a teen, appearance is closely tied to self-esteem, so the nurse acknowledges feelings and redirects safely.
questions.takeaway: Acknowledge feelings, explain the risk, and refer for safe treatment.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Recall why older adults have dry skin and the slide guidance on bathing frequency.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any option that dries or irritates the skin.
questions.stem: An 81-year-old client in assisted living has dry, flaky, itchy skin on the legs and back with scratch marks. No rash or lesions are present. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Apply an alcohol-based lotion to cool the itchy areas
Use a mild, fragrance-free liquid cleanser instead of deodorant soap
Apply an emollient to damp skin right after bathing
Add a scented bath oil to hot bath water to relieve the itching
Keep the client's fingernails short and smooth
Bathe the client twice a day to remove dry flakes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Alcohol dries the skin further.
Correct. Mild, fragrance-free cleansers protect the barrier.
Correct. Moisturizing while the skin is damp locks in water.
Incorrect. Hot water and fragrance dry and irritate the skin.
Correct. Short nails reduce skin damage from scratching.
Incorrect. Older adults bathe every other day; more bathing dries the skin.
questions.rationale: Older skin has fewer oil glands and dries easily. Care follows the independent nursing interventions on the slides: bathe older adults every other day, use mild or liquid cleansers, moisturize after bathing, and prevent scratch damage with short nails.
questions.takeaway: Dry older skin: mild cleanser, moisturize damp skin, short nails, every-other-day bathing.
